extracted.intended_audience: readers of entertainment news; fans and observers of late-night television and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the qualities, innovations, and cultural impact that define influential late-night talk-show comedy, using Letterman's career as the exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-invented the late-night format
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Dave and his writers completely re-invented the format.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative emphasis on structural innovation: did the show change expectations for what a late-night talk show could be (segments, tone, pacing)? Example: by 1985 Letterman’s Late Night was the 'Holy Grail' for aspiring comedy writers because it had altered the genre's shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversive comedic style and unconventional appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Letterman’s “subversive” brand of comedy paired with unlikely television looks (e.g., 'His front teeth had a massive gap that looked almost painted-on as a joke').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the comedian's persona and visual presentation actively undercut mainstream show-business polish and use unconventional aesthetics as part of the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edgy, abstract, or unpalatable humor
rubrics_metrics.description: O’Brien notes his own edgy, abstract humor that at times seemed unpalatable for more mainstream shows like The Tonight Show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider willingness to pursue humor that risks being rejected by mainstream gatekeepers; value placed on originality over immediate mass-appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mocking/skewering celebrity guests
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He amused himself, skewered clueless celebrity guests…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the host treats celebrity culture — whether the show lampoons and exposes celebrity foibles rather than purely flattering guests. Example of an anti-pattern: deferential, fluff interviews that avoid skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive, never-before-seen bits
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Did strange, ironic comedic bits that no one had seen on television before.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize novelty and the introduction of fresh recurring bits or segment concepts. Evaluate whether sketches/segments feel derivative or genuinely original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal, off-kilter tone and reveling in awkwardness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Everything about that show was surreal and off-kilter… this man reveled in awkwardness.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value use of surrealism and purposeful awkwardness as comedic tools, and measure how effectively the show leverages discomfort for humor rather than producing mere discomfort without payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsider stance toward show business
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A big, fat show-business hit that seemingly despised show business… Dave didn’t belong, and he had no interest in belonging.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the performer's positioning relative to industry norms — does the act maintain a critical, outsider voice that adds comedic tension and distinctiveness?

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/long-term impact (‘changed the game’)
rubrics_metrics.description: O’Brien claims no figure in the past 35 years had ‘Dave’s seismic impact on comedy’ and warns against taking that impact for granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate influence by looking at how many comedians cite the figure as formative, how the show’s innovations propagated across the medium, and whether the performer is reasonably described as having 'changed the game' or shifted norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspirational influence for comedians/writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Late Night With David Letterman had been the 'Holy Grail' for several miraculous years, inspiring aspiring writers and comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work serves as a model that other comedians and writers aspire to emulate, demonstrating mentorship via example and setting professional standards.
